/WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 124 AM CST Mon Nov 23 2026

Wednesday, an upper-level ridge will remain established across the 
northern tier of the United States, with a southern-stream trough 
located across the south-central CONUS. Meanwhile, a northern-stream 
shortwave disturbance is expected to develop across the Dakotas 
Wednesday morning before diving southeastward across the region 
through the late morning and early afternoon hours. Increasing 
forcing for ascent associated with an approaching upper-level jet 
streak, mid-level cyclonic vorticity advection, and warm air 
advection (WAA) may support scattered precipitation development 
Wednesday morning into the early afternoon, particularly across 
eastern and northeastern portions of the forecast area. One of the 
primary uncertainties with this system remains the availability and 
depth of moisture. Forecast soundings continue to indicate 
relatively limited moisture through portions of the atmospheric 
column, which may initially inhibit precipitation development or 
result in some precipitation evaporating before reaching the 
surface. However, the combination of increasing large-scale ascent 
and localized saturation associated with the approaching shortwave 
may be sufficient to overcome these moisture limitations and support 
scattered precipitation. Regarding precipitation type, forecast 
thermal profiles currently favor snow as the predominant 
precipitation type, particularly during the morning hours. However, 
with temperatures warming during the day, some rain or a rain/snow 
mix cannot be ruled out depending on the timing of precipitation and 
evolution of the near-surface temperature profile. Given the 
relatively limited moisture availability and localized nature of the 
expected precipitation, any impacts should remain limited at this 
time. Confidence remains lower regarding the exact placement, 
coverage, and intensity of precipitation, which will continue to be 
monitored over the next several forecast cycles. High temperatures 
Wednesday should remain near normal for late November, generally 
reaching the lower to middle 40s across the area.

Thursday into Friday, a stronger upper-level storm system will 
remain positioned across the eastern United States, while upper-
level ridging gradually builds across the central Plains in its 
wake. Northwesterly flow aloft will persist across western and north-
central Nebraska, though increasing mid-level heights and warming 
temperatures in the lower to middle levels should support a gradual 
warming trend. With the stronger forcing for ascent displaced well 
east of the region, mainly dry conditions are expected through the 
latter portion of the workweek. Highs Thursday should begin to 
moderate, with temperatures reaching the lower to middle 50s by 
Friday, which would be above normal for late November.

By the weekend, forecast uncertainty increases as global model 
guidance and associated ensembles suggest another northern-stream 
trough may develop across the northern Plains before progressing 
southeastward into the Midwest. Depending on the eventual strength, 
timing, and western extent of this trough, additional precipitation 
chances could develop across portions of western and north-central 
Nebraska. A farther westward and deeper trough would favor stronger 
forcing for ascent extending into the forecast area, potentially 
supporting greater precipitation chances. Conversely, a more 
easterly track would keep the strongest forcing displaced east of 
the region, limiting precipitation chances and allowing relatively 
milder temperatures to persist. However, considerable uncertainty 
remains regarding the evolution of this system, as global models and 
their associated ensembles continue to differ on the strength and 
placement of the upper-level trough.
